The recursion looks sequential, but the steps combine associatively 

Särkkä & Garcı́a-Fernández, 2021, and so they can run as a parallel scan.
Take a block of steps from s to u.
Describe it by what it says about the state at its end given the state at its start, and about the data in between:p(\vect{x}_u \mid \vect{x}_s, \vect{y}_{s+1:u}) = \mathcal{N}(\vect{x}_u; \mat{F}_\text{cond} \vect{x}_s + \gvect{\mu}_\text{cond}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond}),p(\vect{y}_{s+1:u} \mid \vect{x}_s) \propto \exp\big(-\tfrac{1}{2} \vect{x}_s^\top \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} \vect{x}_s + \vect{b}_\text{lik}^\top \vect{x}_s\big).

These five quantities, with \mat{F}_\text{cond}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond}, \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x} and \gvect{\mu}_\text{cond}, \vect{b}_\text{lik} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}, are an element.
For one step t \ge 2 they are the update of 

(17.4) with \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta as the predicted covariance.
With \gmat{\Sigma}_{y \mid x} = \mat{H}_t \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta \mat{H}_t^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon and \mat{G}_\text{cond} = \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta \mat{H}_t^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{y \mid x}^{-1},\mat{F}_\text{cond} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G}_\text{cond} \mat{H}_t) \mat{F}_t, \qquad \gvect{\mu}_\text{cond} = \mat{G}_\text{cond} \vect{y}_t, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G}_\text{cond} \mat{H}_t) \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta,\vect{b}_\text{lik} = \mat{F}_t^\top \mat{H}_t^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{y \mid x}^{-1} \vect{y}_t, \qquad \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} = \mat{F}_t^\top \mat{H}_t^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_{y \mid x}^{-1} \mat{H}_t \mat{F}_t.

The first step absorbs the prior instead: its \mat{F}_\text{cond}, \vect{b}_\text{lik} and \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} are zero, and its \gvect{\mu}_\text{cond} and \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond} are the filtered moments at t = 1.

To join a block i from s to u with a block j from u to v, integrate out \vect{x}_u.
That Gaussian integral gives\mat{F}_{ij} = \mat{F}_j (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \mat{F}_i, \qquad \gvect{\mu}_{ij} = \mat{F}_j (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} (\gvect{\mu}_i + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \vect{b}_j) + \gvect{\mu}_j,\gmat{\Sigma}_{ij} = \mat{F}_j (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_i \mat{F}_j^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_j,\vect{b}_{ij} = \mat{F}_i^\top (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Lambda}_j \gmat{\Sigma}_i)^{-1} (\vect{b}_j - \gmat{\Lambda}_j \gvect{\mu}_i) + \vect{b}_i, \qquad \gmat{\Lambda}_{ij} = \mat{F}_i^\top (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Lambda}_j \gmat{\Sigma}_i)^{-1} \gmat{\Lambda}_j \mat{F}_i + \gmat{\Lambda}_i,

with the subscript cond or lik dropped.
The first element has \mat{F}_\text{cond} = \mat{0}, so every prefix that starts at it has \mat{F}_{ij} = \mat{0}.
The \gvect{\mu} and \gmat{\Sigma} of such a prefix are the filtered moments at its end.
So an associative scan returns all T filtered marginals, with O(\log T) span given enough processors.

The square-root form of 

Yaghoobi et al. (2025) carries \mat{L}_\text{cond} and \mat{L}_\text{lik} with \gmat{\Sigma}_\text{cond} = \mat{L}_\text{cond} \mat{L}_\text{cond}^\top and \gmat{\Lambda}_\text{lik} = \mat{L}_\text{lik} \mat{L}_\text{lik}^\top.
Each combination triangularises a stack holding an identity,\gmat{\Xi} = \op{tria} \begin{bmatrix} \mat{L}_i^\top \mat{L}_{\text{lik},j} & \mat{I} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mat{M} = \mat{L}_i \gmat{\Xi}^{-\top}, \qquad \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top = (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_i,

where \gmat{\Xi}, \mat{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}.
The factor of 

(17.19) is then \mat{L}_{ij} = \op{tria}([\mat{F}_j \mat{M}, \mat{L}_j]).
gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter(square_root=True) does exactly this, and SquareRootKF is a thin wrapper around it that reports the covariances \mat{L} \mat{L}^\top.
The model covariances are factored once, outside the scan, by a Cholesky of their correlation matrix.
That follows a diagonal shift of 4 D \epsilon, with D the matrix’s side and \epsilon the machine epsilon, so a covariance that is singular only by rounding still factors.

Program 17.3 writes this out in dense numpy for the model above.
It builds the T elements, reduces them from the left and in a balanced tree, and takes one update through 

(17.11).
The two reductions must agree with each other, and with the last filtered moments of SquareRootKF, because the operation is associative and the elements describe the same posterior.

# user
# one element, in the covariance form of the two equations above
def step_element(F, H, Q, R, y):
    innovation = H @ Q @ H.T + R
    gain = np.linalg.solve(innovation, H @ Q).T
    contraction = np.eye(len(F)) - gain @ H
    likelihood_map = H @ F
    weighted = np.linalg.solve(innovation, likelihood_map)
    return (
        contraction @ F,
        gain @ y,
        contraction @ Q,
        likelihood_map.T @ np.linalg.solve(innovation, y),
        likelihood_map.T @ weighted,
    )


# user
# join block i and block j, integrating out the state between them
def combine(first, second):
    F_i, mean_i, cov_i, info_i, prec_i = first
    F_j, mean_j, cov_j, info_j, prec_j = second
    identity = np.eye(len(F_i))
    forward = np.linalg.inv(identity + cov_i @ prec_j)
    backward = np.linalg.inv(identity + prec_j @ cov_i)
    return (
        F_j @ forward @ F_i,
        F_j @ forward @ (mean_i + cov_i @ info_j) + mean_j,
        F_j @ forward @ cov_i @ F_j.T + cov_j,
        F_i.T @ backward @ (info_j - prec_j @ mean_i) + info_i,
        F_i.T @ backward @ prec_j @ F_i + prec_i,
    )


# user
# reduce pairwise, in a balanced tree
def reduce_balanced(elements):
    while len(elements) > 1:
        pairs = zip(elements[0::2], elements[1::2], strict=False)
        joined = [combine(first, second) for first, second in pairs]
        if len(elements) % 2:
            joined.append(elements[-1])
        elements = joined
    return elements[0]


F, H, Q, R = model
data = np.asarray(observations)
# μ_x,1|1 and Σ_x,1|1 from the Joseph filter, for the first element
first_element = (0 * F, dense[0][0], dense[1][0], np.zeros(3), 0 * F)
elements = [first_element] + [step_element(F, H, Q, R, y) for y in data[1:]]

from_left = elements[0]
for element in elements[1:]:
    from_left = combine(from_left, element)
balanced = reduce_balanced(elements)

print(f"{gap(from_left[1], balanced[1]):.0e} {gap(from_left[2], balanced[2]):.0e}")
print(f"{gap(balanced[1], kalman.filtered_means[-1]):.0e}")
print(f"{gap(balanced[2], kalman.filtered_covs[-1]):.0e}")


# user
# L with L Lᵀ = A Aᵀ, from a QR of Aᵀ
def tria(stack):
    upper = np.linalg.qr(stack.T, mode="r")
    signs = np.sign(np.diag(upper))
    return (signs[:, None] * upper).T


# L_x, L_ε
prior_root = np.linalg.cholesky(cov_of_first)
noise_root = np.linalg.cholesky(R)
# Ψ, partitioned at D_y
psi = tria(
    np.block([[H @ prior_root, noise_root], [prior_root, np.zeros((3, 2))]])
)
gain_block, updated_root = psi[2:, :2], psi[2:, 2:]
# G = Ψ₂₁ L_y⁻¹
gain = np.linalg.solve(psi[:2, :2].T, gain_block.T).T
# μ_x,1|1 = μ_x,1|0 + G r₁
residual = data[0] - H @ prior_of_first
print(f"{gap(prior_of_first + gain @ residual, dense[0][0]):.0e}")
print(f"{gap(updated_root @ updated_root.T, dense[1][0]):.0e}")

records.content:
The point of a factor is what happens in float32, and the test of it is the mean.
A covariance can be positive definite while the mean beside it is wrong, and this is not a hypothetical.
Before gaussx v0.6.9 the means of square_root=True were up to billions of standard deviations off on the models below, while the covariances still looked healthy, as tests/test_filters_advanced.py records.

The cause was the mean shift of 

(17.18).
The push-through identity gives (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \vect{v} = \vect{v} - \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \gmat{\Lambda}_j \vect{v}, which subtracts nearly equal vectors when \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j is near 1 / \epsilon.
Applied to \vect{v} = \gmat{\Sigma}_i \vect{b}_j, a large vector, the rounding swamps the answer.
By 

(17.21) the same quantity has a form with nothing to cancel:(\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma}_i \gmat{\Lambda}_j)^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma}_i \vect{b}_j = \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \vect{b}_j.

gaussx uses this for the shift and keeps the push-through only for \gvect{\mu}_i.


Chapter 18 measures the two forms side by side.

Program 17.4 runs the constant-velocity model of those tests, with T = 64 and data drawn from the model, against float64 SquareRootKF as the reference.
It reports the largest mean error in reference standard deviations, the log-likelihood error, and the smallest eigenvalue of the filtered covariances.

# Shapes: T = 64 times; D_x = 2; D_y = 1

# F, constant velocity
velocity_model = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0]])  # → (D_x, D_x)
# H reads the position
position = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0]])  # → (D_y, D_x)


# user
# xₜ = F xₜ₋₁ + ηₜ and yₜ = H xₜ + εₜ, with Σ_η = q I, Σ_ε = r I and Σ_x,0 = p I
def strong_data(q: float, r: float, p: float) -> Float[Array, "time obs"]:
    # user
    def advance(state, key):
        process_key, obs_key = jr.split(key)
        state = velocity_model @ state + jnp.sqrt(q) * jr.normal(process_key, (2,))
        return state, position @ state + jnp.sqrt(r) * jr.normal(obs_key, (1,))

    first = jnp.sqrt(p) * jr.normal(jr.key(0), (2,))
    return jax.lax.scan(advance, first, jr.split(jr.key(1), 64))[1]


# user
# the arguments of every solver, in one precision
def strong_inputs(q, r, p, data, dtype):
    return (
        velocity_model.astype(dtype),
        position.astype(dtype),
        (q * jnp.eye(2)).astype(dtype),
        (r * jnp.eye(1)).astype(dtype),
        data.astype(dtype),
        jnp.zeros(2, dtype),
        (p * jnp.eye(2)).astype(dtype),
    )


# today (filterax)
# jitted, so the three models share one compilation per precision
square_root = jax.jit(
    lambda F, H, Q, R, y, m, P: flx.filters.SquareRootKF(F, H, Q, R).filter(y, m, P)
)
# today (gaussx)
covariance_form = jax.jit(gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter)


# today (filterax)
# the sequential smoother, started from the one-step prediction of the prior
@jax.jit
def sequential(F, H, Q, R, y, m, P):
    return flx.KalmanSmoother(F, Q, H, R, F @ m, predicted_cov(F, P, Q)).smooth(y)


for q, r, p in [(1e-8, 1e-6, 1.0), (1e-10, 1e-8, 1.0), (1e-12, 1e-10, 100.0)]:
    data = strong_data(q, r, p)
    reference = square_root(*strong_inputs(q, r, p, data, jnp.float64))
    # √(diag Σ_x,t|t), from the reference
    deviations = jnp.sqrt(jax.vmap(jnp.diag)(reference.filtered_covs))  # → (T, D_x)
    print(f"q={q:g} r={r:g} p={p:g}, reference {reference.log_likelihood:.3f}")
    for name, solver in [
        ("sqrt", square_root),
        ("cov", covariance_form),
        ("seq", sequential),
    ]:
        single = solver(*strong_inputs(q, r, p, data, jnp.float32))
        error = jnp.abs(single.filtered_means - reference.filtered_means) / deviations
        smallest = jnp.linalg.eigvalsh(single.filtered_covs).min()
        print(
            f"  {name}: {jnp.nanmax(error):.2g} sd, "
            f"{single.log_likelihood - reference.log_likelihood:.3g}, {smallest:.1e}"
        )
    double = sequential(*strong_inputs(q, r, p, data, jnp.float64))
    error = jnp.abs(double.filtered_means - reference.filtered_means) / deviations
    print(f"  float64 seq against sqrt: {error.max():.0e} sd")

records.content:
An ensemble filter on this model has no bias from nonlinearity, so what remains is sampling error, which should fall as 1 / \sqrt{N_\mathcal{E}}.


Program 17.5 measures it.
Each member takes its own draw of \gvect{\eta}_t in the forecast, then filters.ETKF or filters.StochasticEnKF assimilates, and EnKS runs the backward pass.
The numbers are averages over 6 independent runs of the RMS difference from the reference over all components and all T = 40 times.

# Shapes: T = 40 times; D_x = 3; D_y = 2; N_E members; 6 independent runs

# today (lineax)
# Σ_ε = 0.2 I
diagonal_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.2 * jnp.ones(2))  # (D_y, D_y) operator


# user
# h(x) = H x
def observe(state: Float[Array, " state"]) -> Float[Array, " obs"]:
    return obs_model @ state


# user
# one twin run: the forecast and analysis ensembles, and the summed log-likelihood
def ensemble_run(key, num_members, make_filter):
    start_key, run_key = jr.split(key)
    # x⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(μ_x,0, Σ_x,0)
    start = init_mean + jr.normal(start_key, (num_members, 3))  # → (N_E, D_x)

    # user
    def cycle(members, inputs):
        window_key, observed = inputs
        draw_key, filter_key = jr.split(window_key)
        # x⁽ᵉ⁾ ← F x⁽ᵉ⁾ + η⁽ᵉ⁾
        moved = einx.dot(  # → (N_E, D_x)
            "member state, other state -> member other", members, transition
        )
        draws = jr.normal(draw_key, (num_members, 3))  # → (N_E, D_x)
        forecast = moved + einx.dot(  # → (N_E, D_x)
            "other state, member state -> member other", process_root, draws
        )
        # today (filterax)
        analysis = make_filter(filter_key).analysis(
            forecast, observed, observe, diagonal_noise
        )
        outputs = forecast, analysis.particles, analysis.log_likelihood
        return analysis.particles, outputs

    window_keys = jr.split(run_key, num_steps)  # → (T,)
    return jax.lax.scan(cycle, start, (window_keys, observations))[1]


# user
# RMS difference of the ensemble mean and sample covariance from a reference
def errors_against(history, mean, cov):
    # x̄ₜ
    sample_mean = einx.mean("t [member] state", history)  # → (T, D_x)
    # X̃ₜ
    anomalies = einx.subtract(  # → (T, N_E, D_x)
        "t member state, t state -> t member state", history, sample_mean
    )
    # Σ̂ₓ,ₜ
    sample_cov = einx.dot(  # → (T, D_x, D_x)
        "t member state, t member other -> t state other", anomalies, anomalies
    ) / (history.shape[1] - 1)
    mean_error = jnp.sqrt(jnp.mean((sample_mean - mean) ** 2))  # → ()
    cov_error = jnp.sqrt(jnp.mean((sample_cov - cov) ** 2))  # → ()
    return jnp.stack([mean_error, cov_error])  # → (2,)


run_keys = jr.split(jr.key(10), 6)  # → (6,)
rows = {}
for name, make_filter in [
    ("ETKF", lambda _: flx.filters.ETKF()),
    ("EnKF", lambda key: flx.filters.StochasticEnKF(key=key)),
]:
    for num_members in (10, 40, 160, 640):
        # user
        def score(key):
            history = ensemble_run(key, num_members, make_filter)
            forecast, analysis, log_likelihoods = history
            # today (filterax)
            backward = flx.EnKS().smooth(forecast, analysis).smoothed_history
            smooth_moments = smoothed.smoothed_means, smoothed.smoothed_covs
            return (
                errors_against(analysis, kalman.filtered_means, kalman.filtered_covs),
                errors_against(backward, *smooth_moments),
                jnp.abs(jnp.sum(log_likelihoods) - kalman.log_likelihood),
            )

        filtered, backward, evidence = jax.jit(jax.vmap(score))(run_keys)
        rows[name, num_members] = float(jnp.mean(filtered[:, 0]))
        print(
            f"{name} {num_members:3d}: filter {jnp.mean(filtered[:, 0]):.3f} "
            f"{jnp.mean(filtered[:, 1]):.3f}, smoother {jnp.mean(backward[:, 0]):.3f} "
            f"{jnp.mean(backward[:, 1]):.3f}, evidence {jnp.mean(evidence):.2f}"
        )
# the slope of log error against log N_E, from N_E = 10 to N_E = 640
print(f"{np.log(rows['ETKF', 640] / rows['ETKF', 10]) / np.log(64):.2f}")

records.content:
The references are exact for one model class, and they can fail you in the ways below.

Nonlinear or non-Gaussian. SquareRootKF and KalmanSmoother take matrices, so a nonlinear model has no entry point, and the ensemble methods then have no exact reference. Use a grid, as in 

chapter 20.

Scale. The cost is O(T (D_x^3 + D_y^3)) with dense D_x \times D_x matrices, which is why they are references for small problems and not solvers for large ones.

Float32 at extreme conditioning. The table above shows every form losing the mean by the last row.

What the wrapper leaves out. SquareRootKF has one \mat{F}, \mat{H}, \gmat{\Sigma}_\eta and \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon for all times and no mask. For either, call gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter directly.

The prior convention. Giving both classes the same prior is the mistake to expect, and 

Program 17.6 measures it.

# Shapes: T = 40 times; D_x = 3; D_y = 2

# today (filterax)
# the prior of x₀ used as the prior of x₁, which skips one transition
misread = flx.KalmanSmoother(
    transition, process_noise, obs_model, obs_noise, init_mean, init_cov
)
misread_result = jax.jit(lambda y: misread.smooth(y))(observations)
# |μ_x,t|t − μ_x,t|t|, at the first and last times
wrong_filter = jnp.abs(misread_result.filtered_means - kalman.filtered_means)
print(f"{wrong_filter[0].max():.3f} {wrong_filter[-1].max():.0e}")
print(f"{misread_result.log_likelihood - kalman.log_likelihood:.3f}")

Program 17.6:Handing KalmanSmoother the prior of SquareRootKF without predicting it first.

It prints 0.037 7e-04 and 0.171.
The filtered mean is off by 0.037 at the first time and the model has nearly forgotten it by the last, while the log-likelihood stays off by 0.171.
Nothing raises, since both priors are valid.

Use them when the model is linear and Gaussian and you want the answer rather than an estimate of it.
That covers the baseline of a twin experiment, the ground truth of a test for a new filter, and a Gaussian process in time at O(T) through from_sde.
Use SquareRootKF when the covariance must stay positive definite in float32, or when gaussx.parallel_kalman_filter’s scan suits your hardware.
Use KalmanSmoother when you need smoothed marginals, missing data or irregular times.

Reach for an ensemble method when the model is nonlinear or D_x is too large for a dense matrix.

records.content:
Chapter 4: the Kalman update these classes compute

Chapter 6: the ETKF, measured here against the reference

Chapter 10: the ensemble smoothers, which converge to KalmanSmoother

Chapter 18: float32, cancellation and gradients across the library

API: filters and 

smoothers

The algebra of a Kalman update fits on a page, and floating point is where it goes wrong.
The failures of interest raise nothing: the arrays stay finite, the covariance stays positive definite, and the answer is wrong.
A library that wants float32 and gradients has to design around them.

Seven themes recur across filterax and gaussx, and they organise this chapter.
Each one gets a small demonstration, and the chapter ends with the limits that are still open.
Throughout, \epsilon is the machine epsilon, about 1.2 \times 10^{-7} in float32 and 2.2 \times 10^{-16} in float64.

hierarchy.lvl2: Forming a Gram matrix squares the condition number
Forming a Gram matrix squares the condition number

records.content:
Take anomalies \tilde{\mat{X}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_x} with the thin singular value decomposition \tilde{\mat{X}} = \mat{U} \op{diag}(\gvect{\sigma}) \mat{V}^\top, where \gvect{\sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^R is non-negative and sorted down.
The Gram matrix is then\tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\top = \mat{U} \op{diag}(\gvect{\sigma}^2) \mat{U}^\top, \qquad \kappa(\tilde{\mat{X}} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\top) = \kappa(\tilde{\mat{X}})^2,

where \kappa is the ratio of the largest singular value to the smallest.
An eigendecomposition resolves eigenvalues only to about \epsilon \sigma_1^2.
So a singular value below about \sqrt{\epsilon} \sigma_1, which is 3.5 \times 10^{-4} \sigma_1 in float32, is lost once the Gram matrix has been formed, however careful the solver.
Working from \tilde{\mat{X}} itself resolves it down to about \epsilon \sigma_1.

Program 18.1 builds anomalies with \gvect{\sigma} = (1, 10^{-1}, \dots, 10^{-4}) and reads the singular values both ways.
It then takes one backward smoother step, where the smoothed state differs from the forecast along the strongest and the weakest mode.
EnKS calls gaussx.ensemble_rts_step, which takes the pseudo-inverse from the singular values of the anomalies and differentiates it by the closed form of 

Golub & Pereyra (1973).
EnsembleSqrtSmoother forms the Gram matrix instead.

import einx
import filterax as flx
import gaussx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax.random as jr
import lineax as lx
import numpy as np
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# Shapes: N_E = 12 members; D_x = 40 state components; R = 5 modes

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# centred left vectors, so the rows sum to zero as anomalies do
left, _, _ = np.linalg.svd(np.eye(12) - 1.0 / 12.0)
left = left[:, :5]  # → (N_E, R)
right, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(40, 5)))  # → (D_x, R)
# σ = 1, 10⁻¹, …, 10⁻⁴
singular_values = 10.0 ** -np.arange(5.0)  # → (R,)
# X̃ = U diag(σ) Vᵀ, the forecast anomalies
forecast_anomalies = left * singular_values @ right.T  # → (N_E, D_x)
single = jnp.asarray(forecast_anomalies, jnp.float32)  # → (N_E, D_x)

# today (jax)
# σ from X̃
from_matrix = jnp.linalg.svdvals(single)[:5]  # → (R,)
# X̃ X̃ᵀ
gram = einx.dot("member state, other state -> member other", single, single)
# today (jax)
# σ² from X̃ X̃ᵀ, descending
from_gram = jnp.linalg.eigvalsh(gram)[::-1][:5]  # → (R,)
# √max(σ², 0)
from_gram = jnp.sqrt(jnp.maximum(from_gram, 0.0))  # → (R,)
print(np.abs(np.asarray(from_matrix) - singular_values) / singular_values)
print(np.abs(np.asarray(from_gram) - singular_values) / singular_values)

# A backward step from the last time to the first, with a smoothed shift along the
# strongest and weakest modes.
# X_t+1^f
forecast_next = forecast_anomalies + 1.0  # → (N_E, D_x)
# X_t^a
analysis_now = 0.7 * forecast_anomalies + 1.0  # → (N_E, D_x)
# X_t+1^s = X_t+1^f + the shift
smoothed_next = forecast_next + 0.1 * right[:, 0] + 0.01 * right[:, 4]  # → (N_E, D_x)


# user
# X_t^s from one backward step of a smoother, in one precision
def backward_step(smoother, dtype) -> Float[Array, " state"]:
    forecast = jnp.asarray(np.stack([forecast_next, forecast_next]), dtype)
    analysis = jnp.asarray(np.stack([analysis_now, smoothed_next]), dtype)
    # today (filterax)
    history = smoother.smooth(forecast, analysis).smoothed_history
    return einx.mean("[member] state", history[0])  # → (D_x,)


reference = backward_step(flx.EnKS(), jnp.float64)  # → (D_x,)
other = backward_step(flx.EnsembleSqrtSmoother(), jnp.float64)  # → (D_x,)
print(f"{jnp.abs(reference - other).max():.0e}")
shift = np.abs(np.asarray(reference) - analysis_now.mean(0)).max()
for smoother in (flx.EnKS(), flx.EnsembleSqrtSmoother()):
    error = jnp.abs(backward_step(smoother, jnp.float32) - reference).max()
    print(f"{type(smoother).__name__}: {error / shift:.1e}")

The smoothers then print 7e-11, EnKS: 2.8e-04 and EnsembleSqrtSmoother: 9.5e-02.

hierarchy.lvl2: Finite and positive definite do not mean right
Finite and positive definite do not mean right

records.content:
It is tempting to test a float32 filter by asserting that its output is finite and its covariance positive definite.
That check passes on broken code, because the covariance can be right while the mean beside it is not.
The test that catches it compares means and gradients with a float64 reference, and that is what test_square_root_kf_float32_matches_a_float64_reference does.

Program 18.2 has two cases.
The first is the ensemble-space route of the ETKF on noise variances spanning twelve decades, the setting of 

gaussx#785.
The second is the mean shift of the parallel filter from 

chapter 17.
With \gmat{\Sigma} = \mat{L} \mat{L}^\top and \gmat{\Lambda} = \mat{L}_\text{lik} \mat{L}_\text{lik}^\top, both in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}, and \vect{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}, two forms of the same vector are(\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma} \gmat{\Lambda})^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma} \vect{b} = \gmat{\Sigma} \vect{b} - \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \gmat{\Lambda} \gmat{\Sigma} \vect{b} = \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \vect{b}, \qquad \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top = (\mat{I} + \gmat{\Sigma} \gmat{\Lambda})^{-1} \gmat{\Sigma},

where \mat{M} = \mat{L} \gmat{\Xi}^{-\top} comes from a triangular factor \gmat{\Xi} of a stack holding an identity, so it is well defined at any strength.
The first form is the push-through identity, and it subtracts two large vectors whose difference is small.
The second has nothing to cancel.

# Shapes: N_E = 10 members; D_y = 3 observations; D_x = 2 in the second part

# H̃ and y, with noise variances spanning twelve decades
obs_members = rng.normal(size=(10, 3))  # → (N_E, D_y)
target = rng.normal(size=3)  # → (D_y,)
variances = np.array([1e-6, 1.0, 1e6])  # → (D_y,)
# w̄ = Λ_w⁻¹ H̃ Σ_ε⁻¹ r̄, by a dense float64 solve
mapped_mean = obs_members.mean(0)
centred = obs_members - mapped_mean
weighted = centred / variances
dense_precision = 9.0 * np.eye(10) + weighted @ centred.T
expected = np.linalg.solve(dense_precision, weighted @ (target - mapped_mean))
# today (gaussx)
# the ensemble-space route, in float32
weights, transform = gaussx.etkf_transform(
    jnp.asarray(obs_members, jnp.float32),
    jnp.asarray(target, jnp.float32),
    lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.asarray(variances, jnp.float32)),
    low_rank=False,
)
eigenvalues = jnp.linalg.eigvalsh(transform)  # → (N_E,)
print(bool(jnp.isfinite(weights).all() and jnp.isfinite(transform).all()))
print(f"{eigenvalues.min():.1e} {eigenvalues.max():.3f}")
print(f"{np.abs(np.asarray(weights) - expected).max() / np.abs(expected).max():.2f}")


# user
# (I + Σ Λ)⁻¹ Σ b by the push-through form and by M Mᵀ b
def mean_shift(
    root: Float[Array, "state state"],
    lik_root: Float[Array, "state state"],
    information: Float[Array, " state"],
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " state"], Float[Array, " state"]]:
    # A ↦ Aᵀ
    flip = einx.id("row col -> col row", root)  # → (D_x, D_x)
    # Lᵀ L_lik
    cross = flip @ lik_root  # → (D_x, D_x)
    # [Lᵀ L_lik, I]
    stack = jnp.block([[cross, jnp.eye(2, dtype=root.dtype)]])  # → (D_x, 2 D_x)
    # Ξ = tria([Lᵀ L_lik, I]) = Rᵀ, for the QR of the stack's transpose
    upper = jnp.linalg.qr(einx.id("row col -> col row", stack), mode="r")
    xi = einx.id("row col -> col row", upper)  # → (D_x, D_x)
    # Mᵀ = Ξ⁻¹ Lᵀ
    factor_flip = jax.scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(xi, flip, lower=True)
    # M = L Ξ⁻ᵀ
    factor = einx.id("row col -> col row", factor_flip)  # → (D_x, D_x)
    # Σ b = L Lᵀ b, a large vector
    large = root @ (flip @ information)  # → (D_x,)
    # Λ Σ b = L_lik L_likᵀ Σ b
    pulled = lik_root @ einx.dot("state row, state -> row", lik_root, large)
    # (I + Σ Λ)⁻¹ v = v − M Mᵀ Λ v at v = Σ b, which cancels
    pushed = large - factor @ (factor_flip @ pulled)  # → (D_x,)
    # M Mᵀ b, which does not
    direct = factor @ (factor_flip @ information)  # → (D_x,)
    return pushed, direct


lik_root = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.5, 1.0]])  # → (2, 2)
information = np.array([1.0, -2.0])  # → (2,)
base_root = np.array([[3.0, 0.0], [1.0, 2.0]])  # → (2, 2)
for scale in (1e1, 1e3, 1e5):
    root = scale * base_root  # → (2, 2)
    cov, precision = root @ root.T, lik_root @ lik_root.T
    # (I + Σ Λ)⁻¹ Σ b by dense float64 solve
    exact = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(2) + cov @ precision, cov @ information)  # → (2,)
    # the largest eigenvalue of Σ Λ
    strength = np.linalg.eigvals(cov @ precision).real.max()
    results = []
    for dtype in (jnp.float32, jnp.float64):
        pushed, direct = mean_shift(
            jnp.asarray(root, dtype),
            jnp.asarray(lik_root, dtype),
            jnp.asarray(information, dtype),
        )
        for computed in (pushed, direct):
            miss = np.abs(np.asarray(computed) - exact).max() / np.abs(exact).max()
            results.append(f"{miss:.0e}")
    print(f"{strength:.0e}", results)

The push-through error grows like \epsilon times the strength, in either precision, while \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top \vect{b} stays at round-off.
At strength near 1 / \epsilon the float32 push-through has lost the vector completely, and \mat{M} \mat{M}^\top, the covariance beside it, is unaffected.
This was the failure of square_root=True before gaussx v0.6.9, and 

chapter 17 shows the filter with the fix.

Gradients need the same test, against float64 and against a central difference.


Program 18.3 differentiates the log-likelihood of SquareRootKF on a strongly observed model with D_y < D_x, where the likelihood factors are rank deficient.
gaussx handles that with a custom derivative.
With \mat{L} = \mat{A} \mat{Q} from a QR, the tangent is \mathrm{d} \mat{L} = \mathrm{d} \mat{A} \mat{Q}, which drops a term that only rotates \mat{L} and so never changes \mat{L} \mat{L}^\top.
That needs no \mat{R}^{-1}, so it stays finite at low rank.
The same block compares the Jacobian of the ETKF mean weights in the two precisions, at noise variance 

10-8.

# Shapes: T = 32 times; D_x = 2; D_y = 1; N_E = 10 members in the second half

# F, H
velocity = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0]])  # → (D_x, D_x)
position = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0]])  # → (D_y, D_x)


# user
# xₜ = F xₜ₋₁ + ηₜ and yₜ = H xₜ + εₜ, with Σ_η = 10⁻¹⁰ I and Σ_ε = 10⁻⁸ I
def simulate(state, draw):
    state = velocity @ state + 1e-5 * draw[:2]
    return state, position @ state + 1e-4 * draw[2:]


# y_1:T
draws = jr.normal(jr.key(0), (32, 3))  # → (T, 3)
records = jax.lax.scan(simulate, jr.normal(jr.key(1), (2,)), draws)[1]  # → (T, D_y)


# user
# log p(y_1:T) as a function of log σ², with Σ_ε = σ² I
def log_evidence(log_variance: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    dtype = log_variance.dtype
    # today (filterax)
    model = flx.filters.SquareRootKF(
        velocity.astype(dtype),
        position.astype(dtype),
        (1e-10 * jnp.eye(2)).astype(dtype),
        jnp.exp(log_variance) * jnp.eye(1, dtype=dtype),
    )
    start, start_cov = jnp.zeros(2, dtype), jnp.eye(2, dtype=dtype)
    return model.filter(records.astype(dtype), start, start_cov).log_likelihood


at = jnp.log(jnp.asarray(1e-8))  # → ()
evidence_and_slope = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(log_evidence))
step = 1e-5
central = evidence_and_slope(at + step)[0] - evidence_and_slope(at - step)[0]
single_slope = evidence_and_slope(jnp.float32(at))[1]
double_slope = evidence_and_slope(at)[1]
print(f"{double_slope:.4f} {central / (2.0 * step):.4f} {single_slope:.4f}")

# H̃ and y for the mean weights
strong_members = jr.normal(jr.key(2), (10, 3))  # → (N_E, D_y)
strong_target = jr.normal(jr.key(3), (3,))  # → (D_y,)


# user
# w̄ as a function of σ², with Σ_ε = σ² I
def mean_weights(variance: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, " member"]:
    dtype = variance.dtype
    # today (gaussx)
    return gaussx.etkf_transform(
        strong_members.astype(dtype),
        strong_target.astype(dtype),
        lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(variance * jnp.ones(3, dtype)),
    )[0]


jacobian = jax.jit(jax.jacfwd(mean_weights))
double_jacobian = jacobian(jnp.asarray(1e-8))  # → (N_E,)
single_jacobian = jacobian(jnp.float32(1e-8))  # → (N_E,)
jacobian_gap = jnp.abs(single_jacobian - double_jacobian).max()
print(f"{jacobian_gap / jnp.abs(double_jacobian).max():.0e}")

hierarchy.lvl2: A repeated eigenvalue and gap-free derivatives
A repeated eigenvalue and gap-free derivatives

records.content:
Chapter 6 derives this in full, so here is only the point.
\gmat{\Lambda}_w has the eigenvalue c = N_\mathcal{E} - 1 repeated whenever D_y < N_\mathcal{E} - 1, and JAX’s rule for eigh divides by eigenvalue gaps.
A spectral function needs no such division once its divided differences are written in closed form.

# Shapes: N_E = 30 members; D_y = 2 observations

# h⁽ᵉ⁾
mapped = 1.0 + 0.5 * jr.normal(jr.key(0), (30, 2))  # → (N_E, D_y)
# H̃
mapped_anomalies = flx.ensemble_anomalies(mapped)  # → (N_E, D_y)
# H̃ H̃ᵀ
mapped_gram = einx.dot(  # → (N_E, N_E)
    "member obs, other obs -> member other", mapped_anomalies, mapped_anomalies
)


# user
# ∑ sin W, with W = (c Λ_w⁻¹)^½ through jax's rule for eigh
def through_eigh(variance: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # Λ_w = c I + H̃ H̃ᵀ / σ²
    precision = 29.0 * jnp.eye(30) + mapped_gram / variance  # → (N_E, N_E)
    # today (jax)
    # Λ_w = Φ diag(γ) Φᵀ
    gamma, phi = jnp.linalg.eigh(precision)
    # Φ diag(√(c / γ))
    scaled = einx.multiply(  # → (N_E, N_E)
        "member mode, mode -> member mode", phi, jnp.sqrt(29.0 / gamma)
    )
    # W = Φ diag(√(c / γ)) Φᵀ
    root = einx.dot("member mode, other mode -> member other", scaled, phi)
    return jnp.sum(jnp.sin(root))  # → ()


# user
# ∑ sin W, with W from gaussx
def through_gaussx(variance: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(variance * jnp.ones(2))  # (D_y, D_y) operator
    # today (gaussx)
    _, root = gaussx.etkf_transform(mapped, jnp.zeros(2), noise, low_rank=False)
    return jnp.sum(jnp.sin(root))  # → ()


at = jnp.asarray(0.1)
step = 1e-6
central = (through_gaussx(at + step) - through_gaussx(at - step)) / (2.0 * step)
print(f"{through_eigh(at):.6f} {through_gaussx(at):.6f}")
print(f"{jax.grad(through_eigh)(at)} {jax.grad(through_gaussx)(at):.6f} {central:.6f}")

Program 18.4:The same transform differentiated through eigh and through the gap-free rule, at a repeated eigenvalue.

It prints 25.645979 25.645979, then nan -1.521080 -1.521080.
The values agree, and the derivative through eigh is nan while the gap-free rule matches the central difference.

Every eigenvalue of \gmat{\Lambda}_w is at least c, exactly, because \tilde{\mat{H}} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top is positive semi-definite.
A float32 eigendecomposition does not know that.
It resolves eigenvalues only to about \epsilon times the largest, so a strong observation can return a computed \gamma_i far below c, or below zero.
Then \sqrt{c / \gamma_i} is NaN.
That was 

gaussx#790, now closed: the ensemble-space route floors the computed eigenvalues at c.

The floor is safe because it is a bound the exact matrix satisfies, so it can only move an eigenvalue toward the truth.
A floor that is not such a bound changes the answer without saying so.

Program 18.5 reproduces the setting of that issue, with D_y = 30 observations of N_\mathcal{E} = 8 members, where the ensemble-space route is the only one.

# Shapes: N_E = 8 members; D_x = 12 state components; D_y = 30 observations

prior_term = 7.0
# s, r on a line
state_grid = jnp.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 12)  # → (D_x,)
obs_grid = jnp.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 30)  # → (D_y,)
# H, a Gaussian blur of the state
offsets = einx.subtract("obs, state -> obs state", obs_grid, state_grid)  # → (D_y, D_x)
blur = jnp.exp(-0.5 * (offsets / 1.5) ** 2).astype(jnp.float32)  # → (D_y, D_x)

for smallest in (1e-6, 1e-8):
    # Σ_ε, with variances from `smallest` up to 1
    log_range = jnp.linspace(jnp.log10(smallest), 0.0, 30)  # → (D_y,)
    variance = (10.0**log_range).astype(jnp.float32)  # → (D_y,)
    bare_failures, floored_failures, lowest, mean_error, root_error = 0, 0, [], [], []
    for seed in range(5):
        members = jr.normal(jr.key(seed), (8, 12)).astype(jnp.float32)  # → (N_E, D_x)
        obs_members = einx.dot("member state, obs state -> member obs", members, blur)
        goal = jr.normal(jr.key(100 + seed), (30,)).astype(jnp.float32)  # → (D_y,)
        # H̃
        centred = flx.ensemble_anomalies(obs_members)  # → (N_E, D_y)
        # H̃ Σ_ε⁻¹
        weighted = einx.divide("member obs, obs -> member obs", centred, variance)
        # Λ_w = c I + H̃ Σ_ε⁻¹ H̃ᵀ
        inner = einx.dot("member obs, other obs -> member other", weighted, centred)
        precision = prior_term * jnp.eye(8, dtype=jnp.float32) + inner  # → (N_E, N_E)
        # today (jax)
        # Λ_w = Φ diag(γ) Φᵀ
        gamma, phi = jnp.linalg.eigh(precision)
        lowest.append(float(gamma.min()))
        # W = Φ diag(√(c / γ)) Φᵀ, with no floor
        scaled = einx.multiply(
            "member mode, mode -> member mode", phi, jnp.sqrt(prior_term / gamma)
        )
        bare = einx.dot("member mode, other mode -> member other", scaled, phi)
        bare_failures += int(not jnp.isfinite(bare).all())
        # today (gaussx)
        # the same transform, with γ floored at c
        weights, root = gaussx.etkf_transform(
            obs_members, goal, lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(variance)
        )
        finite = jnp.isfinite(weights).all() and jnp.isfinite(root).all()
        floored_failures += int(not finite)
        # Λ_w, w̄ and W by dense float64 solve on the same float32 inputs
        dense_centred = np.asarray(centred, float)
        dense_mean = np.asarray(obs_members, float).mean(0)
        dense_scaled = dense_centred / np.asarray(variance, float)
        dense_precision = prior_term * np.eye(8) + dense_scaled @ dense_centred.T
        expected = np.linalg.solve(
            dense_precision, dense_scaled @ (np.asarray(goal, float) - dense_mean)
        )
        dense_gamma, dense_phi = np.linalg.eigh(dense_precision)
        expected_root = dense_phi * np.sqrt(prior_term / dense_gamma) @ dense_phi.T
        miss = np.abs(np.asarray(weights) - expected).max()
        mean_error.append(miss / np.abs(expected).max())
        root_error.append(np.abs(np.asarray(root) - expected_root).max())
    print(
        f"{smallest:g}: lowest γ {min(lowest):.2f}, no floor {bare_failures} of 5 "
        f"non-finite, gaussx {floored_failures} of 5, w̄ {max(mean_error):.2f}, "
        f"W {max(root_error):.2f}"
    )

It prints:

Here c = 7, so the computed eigenvalue is 69 below its exact bound on the harder row.
The floor fixes what it was meant to fix: nothing is non-finite.
It does not make the answer right: on that row the mean weights are off by nearly four times their own size.
That is relative to a float64 solve on the same inputs.
A floor restores finiteness and not accuracy, and this is the limit 

gaussx#785 tracks.

A derivative written as a sum of terms can cancel just as a value can, and a custom derivative makes the choice of terms yours.
Two patterns appear in gaussx.

The first is a divided difference, which is what the Daleckii-Krein rule of 

chapter 6 divides by.
For \phi(\gamma) = 1 / \gamma it reduces by hand, and the closed form has no difference left in it:\frac{a^{-1} - b^{-1}}{a - b} = \frac{-1}{a b}.

The second is a sum of derivative terms that are large and opposite.
Take the scalar mean weight \bar{w} = \rho / \Lambda with \rho = 1 / \sigma^2 and \Lambda = c + 1 / \sigma^2, all scalars, for a strong observation.
The product rule gives two terms, each near 1 / \sigma^2, whose sum is near -c:\frac{\mathrm{d} \bar{w}}{\mathrm{d} \sigma^2} = \underbrace{-\Lambda^{-1} \frac{\mathrm{d} \Lambda}{\mathrm{d} \sigma^2} \Lambda^{-1} \rho}_{\approx 1 / \sigma^2} + \underbrace{\Lambda^{-1} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} \sigma^2}}_{\approx -1 / \sigma^2} = \Lambda^{-1} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} \sigma^2} (1 - \bar{w}).

Joining them is not enough, since 1 - \bar{w} is still a difference of nearly equal numbers.
The residual has to be reduced as well, and here it has a form with no subtraction:1 - \bar{w} = \frac{c \sigma^2}{1 + c \sigma^2}.

gaussx does this in matrix form for the mean weights of the rank-D_y route.
It combines the three terms of \mathrm{d} \bar{\vect{w}} before evaluating any of them, around an analysis residual that is computed by deflating the strong modes rather than by subtracting.

# Shapes: all scalars

# user
# a float32 scalar
def single(value: float) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    return jnp.asarray(value, jnp.float32)


first = single(1e4)
for gap in (1e-1, 1e-3):
    second = first + single(gap)
    # (a⁻¹ − b⁻¹) / (a − b), evaluated as written
    written = (1.0 / first - 1.0 / second) / (first - second)
    # −1 / (a b), which has no difference in it
    closed = -1.0 / (first * second)
    print(f"{written:.4e} {closed:.4e}")

prior = single(9.0)
for noise_variance in (1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8, 1e-10):
    variance = single(noise_variance)
    # Λ = c + 1 / σ²
    precision = prior + 1.0 / variance
    # ρ = 1 / σ²
    rho = 1.0 / variance
    # dρ = dΛ = −1 / σ⁴
    d_rho = -1.0 / (variance * variance)
    # −Λ⁻¹ dΛ Λ⁻¹ ρ, the first term of dw̄
    term_one = -d_rho * rho / (precision * precision)
    # Λ⁻¹ dρ, the second term
    term_two = d_rho / precision
    # w̄ = Λ⁻¹ ρ
    weight = rho / precision
    # Λ⁻¹ dρ (1 − w̄), the terms joined but the residual still a difference
    joined = d_rho * (1.0 - weight) / precision
    # Λ⁻¹ dρ c σ² / (1 + c σ²), with the residual reduced by hand as well
    reduced = d_rho * (prior * variance / (1.0 + prior * variance)) / precision
    # dw̄/dσ² = −c / (1 + c σ²)², in float64
    exact = -9.0 / (1.0 + 9.0 * noise_variance) ** 2
    print(
        f"{noise_variance:g}: terms {term_one:.3g} {term_two:.3g}, "
        f"apart {term_one + term_two:.4f}, joined {joined:.4f}, "
        f"reduced {reduced:.4f}, exact {exact:.4f}"
    )

hierarchy.lvl2: Scale invariance: normalise before fourth powers
Scale invariance: normalise before fourth powers

records.content:
The Ledoit-Wolf intensity 

Ledoit & Wolf, 2004 is a ratio of two fourth powers of the anomalies,\lambda = \min\left(1, \frac{b^2}{d^2}\right), \qquad d^2 = \Vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x - \mu \mat{I} \Vert_F^2, \qquad b^2 = \frac{1}{N_\mathcal{E}^2} \sum_e \Vert \tilde{\vect{x}}^{(e)} \tilde{\vect{x}}^{(e) \top} - \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x \Vert_F^2,

with \mu = \op{tr}(\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x) / D_x.
Rescaling the ensemble by s scales both b^2 and d^2 by s^4, so \lambda does not change.
The floating-point range does not share that invariance.
Float32 holds about 10^{\pm 38}, so a state of size 

1012 overflows at the fourth power and one of size 

10-12 underflows to zero.
So gaussx.ledoit_wolf_shrinkage divides the anomalies by their largest entry first, under a stop_gradient, because \lambda does not depend on that scale.

# Shapes: N_E = 40 members; D_x = 4 state components

# one shared factor plus noise, so that λ is well inside (0, 1)
shared = jr.normal(jr.key(0), (40, 1))  # → (N_E, 1)
extra = 0.5 * jr.normal(jr.key(1), (40, 4))  # → (N_E, D_x)
correlated = (shared + extra).astype(jnp.float32)  # → (N_E, D_x)


# user
# λ = min(1, b² / d²), evaluating the fourth powers as written
def naive_shrinkage(ensemble: Float[Array, "member state"]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # X̃
    anomalies = flx.ensemble_anomalies(ensemble)  # → (N_E, D_x)
    # Σ̂_x
    sample = einx.dot(  # → (D_x, D_x)
        "member state, member other -> state other", anomalies, anomalies
    ) / (ensemble.shape[0] - 1)
    # μ = tr(Σ̂_x) / D_x
    target_scale = jnp.trace(sample) / ensemble.shape[1]
    # d² = ‖Σ̂_x − μ I‖²_F
    distance = jnp.sum((sample - target_scale * jnp.eye(4, dtype=sample.dtype)) ** 2)
    # x̃⁽ᵉ⁾ x̃⁽ᵉ⁾ᵀ
    outer = einx.multiply(  # → (N_E, D_x, D_x)
        "member state, member other -> member state other", anomalies, anomalies
    )
    # b² = ∑ₑ ‖x̃⁽ᵉ⁾ x̃⁽ᵉ⁾ᵀ − Σ̂_x‖²_F / N_E²
    deviation = jnp.sum((outer - sample) ** 2) / ensemble.shape[0] ** 2
    return jnp.minimum(1.0, deviation / distance)  # → ()


for scale in (1e-12, 1e-6, 1.0, 1e6, 1e12):
    scaled = correlated * jnp.float32(scale)  # → (N_E, D_x)
    # today (filterax)
    # Σ̂_λ and λ
    _, intensity = flx.ledoit_wolf_shrinkage(scaled)
    print(f"{scale:g}: naive {naive_shrinkage(scaled):.4f}, filterax {intensity:.4f}")

hierarchy.lvl2: Infinity times zero: mask before you divide
Infinity times zero: mask before you divide

records.content:
Automatic differentiation multiplies slopes, so an infinite slope meeting a zero gives NaN even where the answer is well defined.
Two patterns cause it.

The derivative of \sqrt{\rho} at \rho = 0 is infinite, and a guard after the root does not help.
jnp.where still differentiates both branches, and the branch it discards contributes \infty \times 0.
The same goes for a division guarded after the fact.
The cure is to mask the argument first, so the unselected branch evaluates at a harmless value.

This pattern recurs across the code.
_root_weights in gaussx masks \rho before the root, for a zero observation weight.
The Ledoit-Wolf code decides the clipped case before dividing, because d^2 = 0 would have an infinite slope.
EKSStableScheduler floors \Vert \mat{S} \Vert_F^2 inside the root, so its gradient stays finite at zero.
And KalmanSmoother replaces a masked datum with jnp.where rather than multiplying by the mask, since a NaN times zero is still NaN.

# Shapes: T = 6 times; D_x = 2; D_y = 2 in the last part


# user
# √ρ, guarded after the fact
def root_after(weight: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    return jnp.where(weight > 0.0, jnp.sqrt(weight), 0.0)


# user
# √ρ, with the argument masked first, as gaussx does
def root_before(weight: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    positive = weight > 0.0
    return jnp.where(positive, jnp.sqrt(jnp.where(positive, weight, 1.0)), 0.0)


# user
# 1 / v, guarded after the fact
def inverse_after(value: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    return jnp.where(value > 0.0, 1.0 / value, 0.0)


# user
# 1 / v, with the argument masked first
def inverse_before(value: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    positive = value > 0.0
    return jnp.where(positive, 1.0 / jnp.where(positive, value, 1.0), 0.0)


zero = jnp.asarray(0.0)
print(jax.grad(jnp.sqrt)(zero), jax.grad(root_after)(zero), jax.grad(root_before)(zero))
print(jax.grad(inverse_after)(zero), jax.grad(inverse_before)(zero))

# F, Σ_η and H
drift = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0]])  # → (D_x, D_x)
small_noise = 0.01 * jnp.eye(2)  # → (D_x, D_x)
identity = jnp.eye(2)  # → (D_y, D_x)
# y, with one entry missing and one time missing entirely
readings = jr.normal(jr.key(0), (6, 2))  # → (T, D_y)
present = jnp.ones((6, 2), dtype=bool).at[2, 1].set(False).at[4, :].set(False)
holes = jnp.where(present, readings, jnp.nan)  # → (T, D_y)


# user
# log p(y) as a function of log σ², with Σ_ε = σ² I
def masked_evidence(log_variance: Float[Array, ""]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    noise = jnp.exp(log_variance) * jnp.eye(2)  # → (D_y, D_y)
    # today (filterax)
    model = flx.KalmanSmoother(
        drift, small_noise, identity, noise, jnp.zeros(2), jnp.eye(2)
    )
    return model.smooth(holes, present).log_likelihood


at = jnp.log(jnp.asarray(0.1))
step = 1e-6
central = (masked_evidence(at + step) - masked_evidence(at - step)) / (2.0 * step)
print(f"{jax.grad(masked_evidence)(at):.6f} {central:.6f}")

Program 18.8:The slopes of √ρ and 1 / v at zero, the masked form of each, and a masked NaN through KalmanSmoother.

It prints inf nan 0.0, then nan 0.0, then 19.608067 19.608067.
The bare root has an infinite slope, the guard after it gives nan, and the mask before it gives 0.0, and likewise for the division.
The gradient through KalmanSmoother with one NaN entry and one fully missing time matches a central difference.

These four issues on gaussx are open as of 7 November 2026, checked with gh issue view.

gaussx#782: nonlinear_kalman_update with joseph=True returns a covariance near 

1019 at a rank-deficient predicted covariance, and its gradient is NaN. filterax’s UKI passes joseph=False to gaussx.sigma_point_kalman_update.

gaussx#783: validate=True on the same function rejects some well-posed float32 updates and misses indefiniteness at small scale, because its threshold does not follow the scale of the rounding. filterax never passes validate=True.

gaussx#785: the ensemble-space route of etkf_transform loses the mean weights in float32 with noise variances spanning many decades, as measured above. With D_y \ge N_\mathcal{E} there is no other route.

gaussx#787: the derivative with respect to an observation weight of exactly zero is 0, where the one-sided derivative is not. The masking above makes it finite, and it does not make it the one-sided value. The issue notes that a compactly supported taper has zero slope at its support radius, so this reaches only a weight optimised directly.

Program 18.9 reproduces the first and the last.

# Shapes: D_x = 3 state components; D_y = 2 observations, in the first part


# Σ − G Σ_y Gᵀ at a rank-one Σ, against the dense form, for both updates
direction = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 0.5])  # → (D_x,)
# Σ = v vᵀ
rank_one = einx.multiply("state, other -> state other", direction, direction)
# H, Σ_ε, μ and y
blend = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0, 0.5], [0.0, 1.0, -1.0]])  # → (D_y, D_x)
coloured = jnp.array([[0.5, 0.1], [0.1, 0.3]])  # → (D_y, D_y)
location = jnp.array([0.3, -0.2, 0.5])  # → (D_x,)
datum = jnp.array([0.4, 0.1])  # → (D_y,)
# Σ Hᵀ
cross = einx.dot("state other, obs other -> state obs", rank_one, blend)
# Σ_y = H Σ Hᵀ + Σ_ε
total = einx.dot("obs state, state other -> obs other", blend, cross) + coloured
# G Σ_y Gᵀ = Σ Hᵀ Σ_y⁻¹ H Σ
reduction = cross @ jnp.linalg.solve(total, einx.id("state obs -> obs state", cross))
dense_update = rank_one - reduction  # → (D_x, D_x)


# user
# ∑ of the updated covariance, as a function of the predicted one
def updated_total(cov: Float[Array, "state state"], joseph: bool) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # today (gaussx)
    updated = gaussx.nonlinear_kalman_update(
        lambda state: blend @ state, location, cov, datum, coloured, joseph=joseph
    )[1]
    return jnp.sum(updated)  # → ()


for joseph in (True, False):
    # today (gaussx)
    updated = gaussx.nonlinear_kalman_update(
        lambda state: blend @ state, location, rank_one, datum, coloured, joseph=joseph
    )[1]
    finite = bool(jnp.isfinite(jax.grad(updated_total)(rank_one, joseph)).all())
    miss = jnp.abs(updated - dense_update).max()
    print(f"joseph={joseph}: error {miss:.1e}, gradient finite {finite}")

# H̃ and y, for the derivative at a zero weight
members = jr.normal(jr.key(0), (10, 3))  # → (N_E, D_y)
goal = jr.normal(jr.key(1), (3,))  # → (D_y,)
unit_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.2 * jnp.ones(3))  # (D_y, D_y) operator


# user
# ∑ sin W as a function of the observation weights ρ
def weighted_loss(rho: Float[Array, " obs"]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # today (gaussx)
    _, root = gaussx.etkf_transform(members, goal, unit_noise, obs_weights=rho)
    return jnp.sum(jnp.sin(root))  # → ()


rho = jnp.array([1.0, 0.5, 0.0])  # → (D_y,)
last = jnp.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])  # → (D_y,)
forward = (weighted_loss(rho + 1e-6 * last) - weighted_loss(rho)) / 1e-6
print(f"{jax.grad(weighted_loss)(rho)[2]:.4f} {forward:.4f}")

Program 18.9:Two of the open limits, reproduced at the pinned gaussx.

It prints joseph=True: error 1.2e+19, gradient finite False, joseph=False: error 1.8e-15, gradient finite True and 0.0000 0.6409.
The last pair is the gradient at a zero weight and a forward difference with a step of 

10-6.

The themes above reduce to a short list for any new method.

Compare float32 with a float64 reference, on the means and on the gradients, not only on finiteness or definiteness.

Include low-rank inputs, noise variances spanning many decades, and a state of extreme scale.

Check a custom derivative against a central difference in float64, at a repeated eigenvalue and at any boundary where a mask or floor acts.

records.content:
A twin experiment is how an ensemble filter is judged honestly: simulate a truth, observe it with noise, assimilate, and compare the analysis with the truth you hid.
This chapter runs one end to end on the Lorenz-96 model 

Lorenz & Emanuel, 1998, which is chaotic and small enough to run in seconds.

Three things organise it.
Small ensembles need treating, and the treatments are inflation, localization, or both.
The honest report is RMSE against spread over several independent twins, including the settings that fail, because a filter that works on one seed may not work on the next.
And a smoother pass on top is not automatically an improvement.

records.content:
The state is \vect{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}, with D_x = 40 sites on a circle.
filterax has no dynamical core, so the model is written out here.
With indices taken cyclically and forcing 8, its tendency at site k is\frac{\mathrm{d} x_k}{\mathrm{d} t} = (x_{k+1} - x_{k-2}) x_{k-1} - x_k + 8,

and a window advances the state by one fourth-order Runge-Kutta step of \Delta t = 0.05.
The twin observes every second site, D_y = 20, with unit noise:\vect{y}_t = \mat{H} \vect{x}_t + \gvect{\varepsilon}_t, \qquad \gvect{\varepsilon}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \mat{I}).

The first ensemble is the true initial state plus Gaussian noise of variance 4, with N_\mathcal{E} members as rows of \mat{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_\mathcal{E} \times D_x}.
Every run has T = 300 windows, and the scores use the last 200, once the filter has settled.
Two scales judge the result: the observation noise of 1, and the standard deviation of the state itself.

import einx
import filterax as flx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax.random as jr
import lineax as lx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float, Key

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# Shapes: T = 300 windows; D_x = 40 sites; D_y = 20 observed sites; N_E members

num_windows = 300
step_size = 0.05


# user
# dxₖ/dt = (xₖ₊₁ − xₖ₋₂) xₖ₋₁ − xₖ + 8, cyclic in k
def tendency(state: Float[Array, " state"]) -> Float[Array, " state"]:
    return (jnp.roll(state, -1) - jnp.roll(state, 2)) * jnp.roll(state, 1) - state + 8.0


# user
# one RK4 step of Δt = 0.05, with the (x, t₀, t₁) signature filterax calls
def rk4(state: Float[Array, " state"], _=None, __=None) -> Float[Array, " state"]:
    k1 = tendency(state)
    k2 = tendency(state + 0.5 * step_size * k1)
    k3 = tendency(state + 0.5 * step_size * k2)
    k4 = tendency(state + step_size * k3)
    return state + step_size / 6.0 * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)


# user
# xₜ₊₁ = f(xₜ), stacked
def advance(state: Float[Array, " state"], _) -> tuple[Array, Array]:
    next_state = rk4(state)
    return next_state, next_state


# x₀ on the attractor, after 1,000 steps from a perturbed rest state
spun_up = jax.lax.fori_loop(  # → (D_x,)
    0, 1000, lambda _, state: rk4(state), 8.0 + jr.normal(jr.key(0), (40,))
)
_, truth = jax.lax.scan(advance, spun_up, length=num_windows)  # → (T, D_x)
# window times
times = step_size * (jnp.arange(num_windows) + 1.0)  # → (T,)
# H selects every second site
sites = jnp.arange(0, 40, 2)  # → (D_y,)
# Σ_ε = I
unit_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(20))  # (D_y, D_y) operator


# user
# h(x) = H x
def observe(state: Float[Array, " state"]) -> Float[Array, " obs"]:
    return state[sites]


# user
# yₜ = H xₜ + εₜ, and a first ensemble x⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(x₀, 4 I), both from one key
def twin_inputs(key: Key[Array, ""], num_members: int) -> tuple[Array, Array]:
    obs_key, start_key = jr.split(key)
    # yₜ
    records = truth[:, sites] + jr.normal(obs_key, (num_windows, 20))  # → (T, D_y)
    # x⁽ᵉ⁾
    start = spun_up + 2.0 * jr.normal(start_key, (num_members, 40))  # → (N_E, D_x)
    return records, start


# the variability of the state over the run
print(f"{jnp.std(truth):.2f}")

Program 19.1:Lorenz-96 by RK4, a true trajectory on the attractor, and noisy observations of every second site.

It prints 3.67, the standard deviation of the truth.
An RMSE near that value means the filter has lost the trajectory and knows nothing beyond the attractor.
An RMSE below 1 means the filter beats the observations at the observed sites, and it must also fill in the unobserved half.

records.content:
The Layer 2 class 

filterax.ETKF composes a dynamics function, the analysis and an optional inflator, and loops over windows in Python.
Its form of the RTPS inflator 

Whitaker & Hamill, 2012 relaxes each site’s spread back toward its forecast value,\sigma^\text{target}_k = (1 - \alpha) \sigma^{t \mid t}_k + \alpha \sigma^{t \mid t-1}_k,

for \alpha \in [0, 1], by rescaling the anomalies at site k and leaving the mean alone.

A Python loop is fine for one run and costly for a sweep, since every window dispatches its own operations.


differentiable_assimilate runs the same cycle as one jax.lax.scan, so it can be compiled once and vectorised over twins.

# Shapes: T = 30 windows in this block; D_x = 40; D_y = 20; N_E = 20

short = 30
records, start = twin_inputs(jr.key(100), 20)  # → (T, D_y), (N_E, D_x)
windows = [(records[t], times[t]) for t in range(short)]
# today (filterax)
# forecast, ETKF analysis, RTPS with α = 0.3, in a Python loop over windows
model = flx.ETKF(dynamics=rk4, obs_op=observe, inflator=flx.RTPS(alpha=0.3))
looped = model.assimilate(start, windows, unit_noise)
# today (filterax)
# the same cycle in one jax.lax.scan
scanned = flx.differentiable_assimilate(
    flx.filters.ETKF(),
    rk4,
    observe,
    start,
    records[:short],
    times[:short],
    unit_noise,
    inflator=flx.RTPS(alpha=0.3),
)
difference = jnp.abs(looped.analysis_history - scanned.analysis_history).max()
print(f"{difference:.0e}")

Program 19.2:The Layer 2 ETKF with RTPS as a Python loop, and the same cycle as a jax.lax.scan.

It prints 3e-14, so the two loops are the same computation, and the sweep below uses the scan.

records.content:
Program 19.3 runs eight independent twins for each setting, with the same truth and different observation noise and first ensembles.
It calls a twin healthy if its RMSE stays under the observation noise of 1.
For the healthy twins it reports the median RMSE and spread, and otherwise the worst RMSE and any NaN.

The LETKF 

Hunt et al., 2007 needs coordinates, and it measures distance in Euclidean terms.
So the sites sit on a circle of circumference 40, with the observations at their sites, which makes distance respect the cyclic domain.
The distance is the straight chord between two points on the circle, so the radius \ell is close to a count of sites when it is small: a chord of 4 spans about 4.07 sites of arc, and a chord of 8 about 8.65. The LETKF drops observations beyond it.

# Shapes: T = 300 windows; D_x = 40; D_y = 20; N_E members; 8 independent twins

# the sites on a circle of circumference 40, so that Euclidean distance respects
# the cyclic domain; state and observation coordinates
angles = 2.0 * jnp.pi * jnp.arange(40.0) / 40.0  # → (D_x,)
state_coords = (40.0 / (2.0 * jnp.pi)) * jax.vmap(  # → (D_x, 2)
    lambda angle: jnp.array([jnp.cos(angle), jnp.sin(angle)])
)(angles)
obs_coords = state_coords[sites]  # → (D_y, 2)
twin_keys = jr.split(jr.key(100), 8)  # → (8,)
settled = 100


# user
# one twin experiment, as one scan
def run_twin(key, num_members, analysis_filter, inflator, **coordinates):
    records, start = twin_inputs(key, num_members)
    # today (filterax)
    return flx.differentiable_assimilate(
        analysis_filter,
        rk4,
        observe,
        start,
        records,
        times,
        unit_noise,
        inflator=inflator,
        **coordinates,
    )


# user
# RMSE of x̄ₜ and RMS spread, over windows `first` to `last`
def score(history, first=settled, last=num_windows):
    window = history[first:last]  # → (T′, N_E, D_x)
    # x̄ₜ
    means = einx.mean("t [member] state", window)  # → (T′, D_x)
    # today (filterax)
    errors = jax.vmap(flx.utils.rmse_vs_truth)(means, truth[first:last])  # → (T′,)
    # today (filterax)
    spreads = jax.vmap(flx.utils.rms_spread)(window)  # → (T′,)
    rmse = jnp.sqrt(jnp.mean(errors**2))  # → ()
    return rmse, jnp.sqrt(jnp.mean(spreads**2))


# user
# run the twins, then print how many stayed under the unit observation noise,
# the median RMSE and spread of those, and the worst RMSE of the rest
def report(label, num_members, analysis_filter, inflator=None, **coordinates):
    results = jax.jit(
        jax.vmap(
            lambda key: run_twin(
                key, num_members, analysis_filter, inflator, **coordinates
            )
        )
    )(twin_keys)
    histories = results.analysis_history  # → (8, T, N_E, D_x)
    finite = einx.all("twin t [member state]", jnp.isfinite(histories))  # → (8, T)
    survived = einx.all("twin [t]", finite)  # → (8,)
    rmse, spread = jax.vmap(score)(histories)  # → (8,), (8,)
    healthy = survived & (jnp.nan_to_num(rmse, nan=jnp.inf) < 1.0)  # → (8,)
    text = f"{label}: {int(healthy.sum())} of 8 healthy"
    if healthy.any():
        text += f", RMSE {jnp.median(rmse[healthy]):.2f}"
        text += f", spread {jnp.median(spread[healthy]):.2f}"
    if (survived & ~healthy).any():
        text += f", worst RMSE {jnp.max(rmse[survived]):.2f}"
    if (~survived).any():
        first_bad = jax.vmap(jnp.argmin)(finite)[~survived]
        text += f", {int((~survived).sum())} NaN at {sorted(first_bad.tolist())}"
    print(text)
    return results


letkf_coords = {"state_coords": state_coords, "obs_coords": obs_coords}
# today (filterax)
etkf_filter = flx.filters.ETKF()
report("N_E=20 ETKF", 20, etkf_filter)
for alpha in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9):
    rtps = flx.RTPS(alpha=alpha)
    rtps_results = report(f"N_E=20 ETKF RTPS {alpha}", 20, etkf_filter, rtps)
    if alpha == 0.3:
        inflated = rtps_results
letkf_results = report(
    "N_E=20 LETKF 8", 20, flx.filters.LETKF(radius=8.0), **letkf_coords
)
calibrated_results = report(
    "N_E=20 LETKF 8 RTPS 0.2",
    20,
    flx.filters.LETKF(radius=8.0),
    flx.RTPS(alpha=0.2),
    **letkf_coords,
)
report(
    "N_E=20 LETKF 8 RTPS 0.9",
    20,
    flx.filters.LETKF(radius=8.0),
    flx.RTPS(alpha=0.9),
    **letkf_coords,
)
report("N_E=20 LETKF 4", 20, flx.filters.LETKF(radius=4.0), **letkf_coords)
report("N_E=10 ETKF RTPS 0.3", 10, etkf_filter, flx.RTPS(alpha=0.3))
report("N_E=10 LETKF 8", 10, flx.filters.LETKF(radius=8.0), **letkf_coords)
report("N_E=10 LETKF 4", 10, flx.filters.LETKF(radius=4.0), **letkf_coords)
report(
    "N_E=10 LETKF 8 RTPS 0.2",
    10,
    flx.filters.LETKF(radius=8.0),
    flx.RTPS(alpha=0.2),
    **letkf_coords,
)

The two that survive have an RMSE of 0.38 against a spread of 0.25, so they are overconfident as well.

Inflation alone has a narrow window at this size.
At \alpha = 0.5 every twin survives, with RMSE and spread nearly equal.
But \alpha = 0.3 loses one twin, \alpha = 0.7 loses three, and \alpha = 0.9 loses all of them.
Choosing \alpha from a single seed would be unsafe here, because 0.3 gives the lowest RMSE of the three and also fails once.

Localization alone is enough at 20 members, with the lowest RMSE here and every twin healthy.
The spread of 0.28 is a little under the RMSE of 0.32, and adding RTPS at \alpha = 0.2 brings it to 0.35, at the same RMSE.

At 10 members a wide radius is not enough alone, as the LETKF at \ell = 8 without inflation fails 6 of 8.
A tighter radius recovers 7 of 8, and inflation with the wide radius recovers all 8, at an RMSE of 0.33.
The global ETKF with RTPS at \alpha = 0.3 fails on all 8.

# Shapes: T = 300 windows; D_x = 40; D_y = 20; N_E = 20

records.content:
A smoother uses later observations to refine earlier states.
EnKS takes the forecast and analysis histories and walks back over all the windows, and 

FixedLagSmoother stops each backward walk after lag steps.
With \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t} and \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t} the analysis and forecast anomalies, one backward step on the members is\mat{X}_{t \mid T} = \mat{X}_{t \mid t} + (\mat{X}_{t+1 \mid T} - \mat{X}_{t+1 \mid t}) \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t+1 \mid t}^{+} \tilde{\mat{X}}_{t \mid t},

where ^{+} is the pseudo-inverse.
The sample gain here has no localization, whichever filter produced the history.

Program 19.5 scores the windows from 100 to 250, so that every window has later data to use.
It reports medians over the eight twins, because one diverged twin dominates a mean.

# Shapes: T = 300 windows; D_x = 40; N_E = 20; 8 twins

interior = (settled, 250)


# user
# smooth one twin and score it, over the interior windows
def smoothed_score(smoother, forecast, analysis):
    # today (filterax)
    history = smoother.smooth(forecast, analysis).smoothed_history
    return jnp.stack(score(history, *interior))  # → (2,)


# user
# median (RMSE, spread) over the eight twins, since one diverged twin dominates a mean
def median_over_twins(scores: Float[Array, "twin 2"]) -> Float[Array, " 2"]:
    return jax.vmap(jnp.median, in_axes=1)(scores)  # → (2,)


# user
# median (RMSE, spread) of a smoother
def smoother_score(smoother, results):
    scores = jax.vmap(lambda f, a: smoothed_score(smoother, f, a))(
        results.forecast_history, results.analysis_history
    )
    return median_over_twins(scores)  # → (2,)


# user
# median (RMSE, spread) of the filter, over the same windows
def filter_score(results):
    return median_over_twins(  # → (2,)
        jax.vmap(lambda history: jnp.stack(score(history, *interior)))(
            results.analysis_history
        )
    )


for label, results in [
    ("LETKF 8", letkf_results),
    ("LETKF 8 RTPS 0.2", calibrated_results),
]:
    rmse, spread = filter_score(results)
    print(f"{label} filter: {rmse:.3f} {spread:.3f}")
    rmse, spread = smoother_score(flx.EnKS(), results)
    print(f"{label} EnKS: {rmse:.3f} {spread:.3f}")
    for lag in (2, 10, 40):
        rmse, spread = smoother_score(flx.FixedLagSmoother(lag=lag), results)
        print(f"{label} lag {lag}: {rmse:.3f} {spread:.3f}")
# the global ETKF with RTPS at α = 0.3
rmse, spread = filter_score(inflated)
print(f"ETKF RTPS 0.3 filter: {rmse:.3f} {spread:.3f}")
for smoother in (flx.EnKS(), flx.FixedLagSmoother(lag=10)):
    rmse, spread = smoother_score(smoother, inflated)

records.content:
The ensemble Kalman processes of 

chapter 9 solve inverse problems without gradients of the forward model.
They are built on a Gaussian update, so on a nonlinear problem it matters what each one actually returns.
This chapter runs them on a problem small enough to have a grid reference, and measures what each gets right and wrong.

Three questions organise it.
What does each method return next to the true posterior on one nonlinear problem?
Which of its errors are there even when the problem is linear, and can be worked out by hand?
And what happens when the posterior has two modes, which no Gaussian update can represent?

records.content:
The unknown \gvect{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_\theta} with D_\theta = 2 sets the amplitude and the decay rate of a curve, on a log scale so both stay positive.
It is observed at D_y = 5 times \tau_j:g_j(\gvect{\theta}) = \exp(\theta_1) \exp\big(-\exp(\theta_2) \tau_j\big), \qquad \vect{y} = g(\gvect{\theta}) + \gvect{\varepsilon}, \qquad \gvect{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \sigma^2 \mat{I}),

with \sigma = 0.4 and \gvect{\theta}_\text{true} = (0.5, -0.5).
That noise is large against the curve, so the posterior is visibly non-Gaussian.
The prior is \gvect{\theta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \mat{I}), which gives\log p(\gvect{\theta} \mid \vect{y}) = -\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2} \Vert \vect{y} - g(\gvect{\theta}) \Vert^2 - \frac{1}{2} \Vert \gvect{\theta} \Vert^2 + \text{const}.

In two dimensions this needs no sampling, since 

Program 20.1 evaluates it on a grid of 801 \times 801 points.
The same block defines the scores used below: the mean, the standard deviations, the correlation and the skewness of each marginal.
It also scores the distance of the mean from the grid’s, in posterior standard deviations.
The last score is \mathrm{KL}(p \Vert q), from the grid to a Gaussian q with the method’s mean and covariance.

import einx
import filterax as flx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax.random as jr
import lineax as lx
import numpy as np
import optax
from filterax.processes import EKS_Process
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

# Shapes: D_θ = 2 parameters; D_y = 5 observations; N_E members

# τ, the observation times
times = jnp.array([0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0])  # → (D_y,)
noise_std = 0.4


# user
# g(θ) = exp(θ₁) exp(−exp(θ₂) τ)
@jax.jit
def forward(theta: Float[Array, " param"]) -> Float[Array, " obs"]:
    return jnp.exp(theta[0] - jnp.exp(theta[1]) * times)  # → (D_y,)


# y = g(θ_true) + ε
theta_true = jnp.array([0.5, -0.5])  # → (D_θ,)
data = forward(theta_true) + noise_std * jr.normal(jr.key(0), (5,))  # → (D_y,)
# today (lineax)
# Σ_ε = σ² I
noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(noise_std**2 * jnp.ones(5))  # (D_y, D_y) operator
# Σ_θ = I
prior_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2))  # (D_θ, D_θ) operator
prior_mean = jnp.zeros(2)  # → (D_θ,)

# the unnormalised log posterior on a grid of 801 × 801 points, in dense numpy
axis = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, 801)
first, second = np.meshgrid(axis, axis, indexing="ij")
curves = np.exp(first[..., None] - np.exp(second[..., None]) * np.asarray(times))
misfit = ((np.asarray(data) - curves) ** 2).sum(-1) / noise_std**2
log_density = -0.5 * misfit - 0.5 * (first**2 + second**2)
density = np.exp(log_density - log_density.max())
density = density / density.sum()
grid = np.stack([first.ravel(), second.ravel()], 1)
weights = density.ravel()


# user
# mean, covariance and marginal skewness of weighted points, in dense numpy
def moments(points, point_weights=None):
    count = len(points)
    if point_weights is None:
        point_weights = np.full(count, 1.0 / count)
    mean = point_weights @ points
    centred = points - mean
    cov = (centred * point_weights[:, None]).T @ centred
    skew = (point_weights @ centred**3) / np.diag(cov) ** 1.5
    return mean, cov, skew


# user
# KL(grid ‖ 𝒩(m, C)), by summation over the grid
def kl_from_grid(mean, cov):
    centred = grid - mean
    quadratic = (centred * np.linalg.solve(cov, centred.T).T).sum(1)
    log_gaussian = -0.5 * (quadratic + np.linalg.slogdet(2.0 * np.pi * cov)[1])
    cell = (axis[1] - axis[0]) ** 2
    positive = weights > 0
    log_ratio = np.log(weights[positive] / cell) - log_gaussian[positive]
    return float(weights[positive] @ log_ratio)


grid_mean, grid_cov, grid_skew = moments(grid, weights)
grid_std = np.sqrt(np.diag(grid_cov))
grid_map = grid[np.argmax(weights)]


# user
# one row of the table: mean, standard deviations, correlation, skewness and KL
def row(label, mean, cov, skew=None):
    std = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
    shift = np.abs(mean - grid_mean) / grid_std
    text = f"{label}: mean {np.round(mean, 3)}, sd {np.round(std, 3)}"
    text += f", corr {cov[0, 1] / (std[0] * std[1]):.3f}, off {np.round(shift, 2)} sd"
    if skew is not None:
        text += f", skew {np.round(skew, 2)}"
    print(text + f", KL {kl_from_grid(mean, cov):.3f}")


row("grid", grid_mean, grid_cov, grid_skew)
print(f"MAP {np.round(grid_map, 2)}")

Program 20.1:A decay curve with two unknowns, and its posterior on a dense grid.

It prints:

grid: mean [ 0.386 -0.827], sd [0.244 0.529], corr 0.567, off [0. 0.] sd, skew [-0.31 -0.32], KL 0.045

MAP [ 0.45 -0.77]

The posterior is skewed, so its mean and its mode differ, by about a quarter of a standard deviation in \theta_1.
The KL 0.045 is a floor: it is the distance to the Gaussian with the posterior’s own mean and covariance, the best any Gaussian method can do.

records.content:
All three methods are Layer 2 models with a run method, and all start from the prior.

EKI 

Iglesias et al., 2013 moves an ensemble with a tempered Kalman update until the artificial time reaches 1, with steps from DataMisfitController 

Iglesias & Yang, 2021. It has no prior term, so the prior enters only through the first ensemble.

UKI 

Huang et al., 2022 keeps a mean and a covariance, and evaluates g at 2 D_\theta + 1 sigma points in each step, with the same scheduler.

EKS 

Garbuno-Inigo et al., 2020 adds a prior drift and ensemble-scaled noise to the EKI update, so that its ensemble samples rather than collapses. We discard the first 100 of its 200 iterations and pool the rest.

TEKI 

Chada et al., 2020 is here too, as a check on the mode, because it treats the prior as data and targets the MAP.
EKS is the only stochastic method, so it also runs from a second seed, and once with twice the members and target_stiffness = 0.03 for 1,500 iterations.
Those two use the Layer 1 EKS_Process in a jax.lax.scan, because the Layer 2 loop is too slow for that many steps.

# Shapes: N_E = 100 members; D_θ = 2; D_y = 5; N_iter iterations

# θ⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
start = jr.normal(jr.key(1), (100, 2))  # → (N_E, D_θ)

# today (filterax)
# EKI, with the data misfit controller, stopping at t = 1
eki = flx.EKI(forward_fn=forward, obs=data, noise_cov=noise).run(start)
row("EKI", np.asarray(eki.mean), np.asarray(eki.covariance.as_matrix()))
print(f"  {eki.n_iterations} iterations")

# today (filterax)
# UKI, with 2 D_θ + 1 sigma points in each iteration
uki = flx.UKI(forward_fn=forward, obs=data, noise_cov=noise).run(prior_mean, prior_cov)
row("UKI", np.asarray(uki.mean), np.asarray(uki.covariance.as_matrix()))
print(f"  {uki.n_iterations} iterations")

# today (filterax)
# TEKI, the prior as data, which targets the MAP
teki_config = flx.ProcessConfig(
    scheduler=flx.FixedScheduler(dt=1.0), n_iterations=60
)
teki = flx.TEKI(
    forward_fn=forward,
    obs=data,
    noise_cov=noise,
    prior_mean=prior_mean,
    prior_cov=prior_cov,
    config=teki_config,
).run(start)
print(f"TEKI: mean {np.round(np.asarray(teki.mean), 3)}")

# today (filterax)
# EKS with a prior, 200 iterations, sampling after the first 100
eks_config = flx.ProcessConfig(scheduler=flx.EKSStableScheduler(), n_iterations=200)
# today (filterax)
eks = flx.EKS(
    forward_fn=forward,
    obs=data,
    noise_cov=noise,
    prior_mean=prior_mean,
    prior_cov=prior_cov,
    seed=0,
    config=eks_config,
).run(start)
tail = np.asarray(eks.history_particles[100:]).reshape(-1, 2)
row("EKS", *moments(tail))
print(f"  t = {eks.history_algo_time[-1]:.1f}")


# user
# the same sampler at Layer 1, as one scan, keeping the last half of its iterations
def eks_tail(num_members, target_stiffness, iterations, seed):
    scheduler = flx.EKSStableScheduler(target_stiffness=target_stiffness)
    # today (filterax)
    process = EKS_Process(
        scheduler=scheduler, key=seed, prior_mean=prior_mean, prior_cov=prior_cov
    )
    first_members = jr.normal(jr.key(1 + seed), (num_members, 2))  # → (N_E, D_θ)

    # user
    # one EKS update
    def advance(state, _):
        evaluated = jax.vmap(forward)(state.particles)  # → (N_E, D_y)
        state = process.update(state, evaluated)
        return state, state.particles

    initial = process.init(first_members, data, noise)
    _, history = jax.lax.scan(advance, initial, length=iterations)
    return history[iterations // 2 :]  # → (N_iter / 2, N_E, D_θ)


for label, settings in [
    ("EKS, another seed", (100, 0.1, 200, 1)),
    ("EKS, 200 members, smaller steps", (200, 0.03, 1500, 0)),
]:
    samples = jax.jit(lambda: eks_tail(*settings))()
    row(label, *moments(np.asarray(samples).reshape(-1, 2)))

EKS’s skewness is [-0.19 -0.19], [0.03 0.06] and [ 0.01 -0.1 ] in the three runs, against the grid’s [-0.31 -0.32].

Each method is wrong in its own way.

EKI gets the mean closest, at very little cost, and its spread is not a posterior: the standard deviation of \theta_1 is 0.353 against 0.244.

UKI is the cheapest by far, with the widest covariance, 40% to 50% too wide on both parameters, and it cannot represent skew.

EKS gets the standard deviations closest, within about 13%, and has the lowest KL of the three. Its mean of \theta_1 sits at the mode rather than the posterior mean, a quarter to a third of a standard deviation off. Its skewness is too small, and it varies between runs.

The shift in \theta_1 is not sampling noise or step size.
The values 0.459, 0.443 and 0.458 all sit near the MAP of 0.45, including the run with more members and smaller steps.
The update uses ensemble statistics in place of \nabla g, which is exact only for a linear g 

Garbuno-Inigo et al., 2020.
That is the likely source, though we have not isolated it.
